source_title: Giancarlo Esposito Says He ‘Hated’ John Turturro While Filming Their 1989 Spike Lee Comedy - People.com
source_excerpt:
The two are now reuniting in ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,’ in limited theaters now
Steve Granitz/FilmMagic; Jamie McCarthy/Getty
Giancarlo Esposito “hated” John Turturro when they first met for Spike Lee’s Do the Right Thing in the late ‘80s
They eventually became like “family” on the set of their upcoming crime movie, The Only Living Pickpocket in New York
The Only Living Pickpocket in New York is in limited theaters now before expanding on Friday, Oct. 30
Giancarlo Esposito and John Turturro didn’t get off to the best start with each other.
In an exclusive interview with The Hollywood Reporter published on Wednesday, Oct. 28, the Breaking Bad alum, 68, admitted he “hated” the Severance actor, 69, when they first met on set in the late ‘80s.
“I hated him on Do the Right Thing , to be honest with you, and he probably hated me to a certain extent,” Esposito said while laughing as he recalled their time together on the Spike Lee production.
“But I loved him all in the same emotional feeling because I recognized him,” he added.
Esposito didn’t reveal what it was that caused their rift, but the two crossed paths several more times for projects like Lee’s Mo’ Better Blues (1990) and Jungle Fever (1991).
Now, the pair are teaming up for their upcoming crime movie, The Only Living Pickpocket in New York .
The film, which marks Turturro’s first lead role in a major film in more than 20 years, follows Harry Lehman (Turturro), an old-school, smartphone-free transit pickpocket in a 36-hour race across New York City. At one point, he enlists the help of Detective Warren (Esposito), a veteran petty crime cop and old acquaintance of Harry.
Esposito told THR that the Noah Segan-directed film brought them even closer.
“We were on the set of Pickpocket in Detective Warren’s office, and in the middle of a take, he took a deep breath. I knew he hadn’t forgotten his lines. He’s a consummate professional, as I am, but he just had to stop,” the Mandalorian star said.
“And in the middle of a take, he stared into my eyes and said, ‘You’re my uncle. You’re my father. You’re my family.’ And it brought tears to my eyes because I felt the same way. We’re both Italian, and we’re linked somehow in our genetic structure, in who we are and where we come from. So he had to acknowledge that for a minute because he had this déjà vu of being in a room with all of his family,” he continued.
Esposito added, “There’s something about working with someone who’s very present as an actor that I always welcome and wish to have. But I realize that I can only see you if I’m very present and willing to show you who I am. And if you can see me, then you can see yourself as well. So there’s a mirror reflection going on, and that makes for a good partnership on screen.”
Jon Pack/Courtesy of Sony Pictures Classics
Turturro recently spoke to PEOPLE about the role, which he said he was “very happy” about because it was “very human.”
“A lot of people go into that world because they come from broken backgrounds, broken families, orphanages and they find a family,” he said of his character’s pickpocket status.
He added that Harry is “a man who is struggling to survive as the world around him changes.”

“It was a very moving script and very human, and told within this tense thriller structure, which is the guy steals from the wrong person and it takes place in like 36 hours. But there’s a lot of tenderness against the tension.”
Turturro said, “I’m very happy to be in something like that, because it has a lot of humanity.”
The Only Living Pickpocket in New York is in limited theaters now before expanding on Friday, Oct. 30.
